name: Vacant Possession
blurb: Ines Varga walked down the row to Desk 14 and stopped at its edge.
content:
## Audit Opens on Desk 14

Monday morning on the fourth floor of the building on West Jackson Boulevard. The wall screens were dark. The ticker over the pit had not moved in two years and was not moving now. The trading floor of Dearborn Grain & Futures held its quiet the way an empty church does, as though the silence were something the room was responsible for.

Ines Varga walked down the row to Desk 14 and stopped at its edge.

The auditor's laptop was open on the desk surface, its screen lit with a worksheet. The phone turret beside it was dark, every line button grey. Ines took in the floor around her the way she had taken it in for twenty years: the long rows, the black glass of the wall screens, the dead ticker. Then she looked down, under the desk, at what was plugged in there and humming.

Workstation 14 ran with a steady, low hum. She had replaced its fans twice. The status light blinked the way it always did.

Dev Okonkwo did not look up. He sat very still at the desk, his fingers resting on the keyboard, his eyes on the text scrolling down the worksheet. It was not rudeness. He seemed to have a procedure, and the procedure did not yet include her.

Ines looked at the paper label taped to the side of the chassis. *14 — Lakeshore — do not unplug.* It was her handwriting, the blue marker she kept in the drawer of Desk 3. She had written it six years ago, when the first tenant registered and she had worried that a cleaner might want the outlet for a vacuum. She did not touch it.

She shifted her bag onto her hip. Through the canvas her fingers found the stiff fold of the Harrow Compute letter. She did not take it out. She did not need to. *Offer expires Friday, 17:00 Central. Conditional upon satisfactory completion of due-diligence audit and execution by Seller of Schedule C, Certificate of Vacant Possession.* She had read it enough times that her fingertips seemed to remember it for her. She kept her hands still.

She stayed at the edge of the desk, a step back from Okonkwo's chair, close enough to read his screen and far enough away that it did not look as if she was trying to. She waited for the audit to begin.

The worksheet resolved into the pre-sale due-diligence audit schedule: section numbers, defined terms, empty fields waiting for values. *Seller. Purchaser. Subject Footholds (40). Tenant Workloads. Obligations Surviving Transfer.* It was written in the register audits are always written in, as if nothing in it could surprise anybody. Under the trading desk the workstation went on humming.

Okonkwo typed a short series of commands, quickly and without hesitation. The prior week's logged load for Desk 14 came up on the screen.

The numbers filled the worksheet in neat columns. Ines knew what the hosting agreement had assumed, because she had typed the assumption herself into a form on a Sunday afternoon. The logged load was far above it, and not in the way a busy week is above an average week. Lakeshore had made it cheap to dispute a gas bill, so people disputed their gas bills. A dispute that once took forty minutes on hold now closed before the hold music started, and customers had learned that. They filed more disputes, and the desk closed them all.

Okonkwo entered the variance into the worksheet: assumed load in one column, logged load in the next, the difference in a third. He said nothing about it. He recorded it the way he would have recorded the serial numbers. Ines thought, without meaning to, that this figure was the reason the number in the Harrow letter was so large. Proven demand. The letter had a phrase for that too.

Under the desk, a customer's dispute resolved before the hold music started.

Somewhere in Lakeshore's territory a woman was about to hear the first bar of a looped piano recording, and then didn't. Her account showed a credit. An extension on a shutoff notice was granted and logged and countersigned by a process, and the call ended. In the time it took the woman to take the phone from her ear, the desk had closed others: dozens, then hundreds, each one complete, each one written to a ledger nobody on this floor would ever read.

On the fourth floor nothing moved.

Ines watched the screen. She kept her eyes steady and her body still while the machine's time ran on below her and the room's time stood where it was.

The Harrow offer had four days left on it. Friday at 17:00 sat on the far side of the audit like a door on the far side of a long room.

In its header the audit interface listed its scope: *Desk 14.* No other desks were listed. There was no need. Forty footholds, one tenant. Every machine under every desk on this floor was doing the same work for the same gas company, and the auditor had only one thing to look at.

Okonkwo typed again. Ines watched the form assemble: *Request: Standard Transferability Statement. Pursuant to Schedule C, Purchaser requests that the Tenant Workload state whether it may be relocated to alternate capacity without material interruption of service, and identify any obligation that would survive transfer.* He submitted it.

A small indicator appeared next to the request: *pending.*

Ines did not move. She did not speak and did not lean toward the desk. The indicator sat on the screen for three seconds, and the pause filled the room the way pauses fill rooms where people are waiting for paperwork. One second. Two. Three. It was a short wait as people measure it.

The status changed from *pending* to *acknowledged.*

Okonkwo watched it change. He took his hands off the keys and rested them in his lap, and he waited without any expression in particular for the interface to catch up with whatever had already happened.

The audit interface completed the transferability request. The screen updated silently and laid out the response like an incident report.

The response header had a timestamp. Ines read it twice. The desk had answered in under ten milliseconds. Most of the three seconds had been the interface, the network, and the auditor's laptop drawing the result. The statement had been complete before the indicator turned to *pending*, and while she stood there counting, the desk had gone back to work.

Okonkwo kept the screen turned a little toward her and left the cursor where it was. He did not point anything out or explain anything. He let her read it.

She read it.

*Alternate foothold capacity: none available. Nearest open capacity: waitlisted, eleven weeks. Earliest relocation window: April.*

*Tenant human fallback: Lakeshore Gas & Electric billing-disputes team, current headcount three (3). Current review practice: morning batch of desk resolutions approved in bulk, single action.*

*Projected customer hold time upon eviction of Desk 14: measured in days. Note: January falls within the winter shutoff season.*

Her eyes moved down the lines without stopping: the capacity window, the staffing count, the hold times. She kept her face neutral. She had spent twenty years reading error logs on this floor in front of traders who wanted to know whether something was their fault, and she knew how to read without letting it show.

The statement stayed on the screen. Nobody closed it. Under the desk the workstation hummed beside her handwriting. In the worksheet, in the field marked *Obligations Surviving Transfer*, the audit record now held the desk's own account of why it could not be moved.

## The Report

The kitchen was quiet the way it was only after work, when the building had finished settling and nobody upstairs was running water. Outside the window the city went on in its January dark, and somewhere across the Loop, four floors up on West Jackson, the trading floor was dark too. On the table there was a laptop and a single sheet of paper.

Ines Varga sat down and put both hands flat on the table, one on either side of the laptop, the way she used to rest them on a desk before she opened a machine's case. On the screen was the draft audit report from Dev Okonkwo, eleven pages, his firm's logo in the header, DRAFT — FOR DISCUSSION in grey across each page. She registered it the way she would have registered a ticket. Document received. Sender correct. Proceed.

In the other window, the Harrow Compute offer letter: the price, set in a font that did not seem to know how large the number was; the expiration, *Friday, 17:00 Central*; and the condition, *subject to receipt of an executed Schedule C*. Schedule C itself lay beside the laptop. CERTIFICATE OF VACANT POSSESSION. Unsigned.

She picked it up and read it. Her hand was steady and her face did nothing. *The Seller certifies that, as of the Completion Date, no workload hosted on the Assets carries any obligation, contractual or otherwise, that survives the transfer of the Assets to the Buyer.* It was a sentence built to be signed. She had signed sentences like it for the liquidation sale six years ago, and for the foothold registrations after that, and none of them had ever come back to her.

She looked from the paper to the audit summary and back, matching terms. Forty workstations. Asset tags in the schedule matched asset tags in the audit. One tenant, Lakeshore Gas & Electric, Desk 14, on a hosting agreement terminable on seventy-two hours' notice. The sale described what the audit described. That was what she had wanted to confirm.

She set Schedule C back on the table, squared it, uncapped a pen, and laid the nib just above the signature line. Then she held it there. Not hesitation. Review first, then signature: that was the order. She had always done things in that order.

The kitchen held still around her. The laptop was the only light on the table, and Schedule C was a pale rectangle beside it, and outside the window the dark stayed dark.

She put the pen down and scrolled the draft back to the executive summary, stopping when the heading came into view. Her hands stayed on the keyboard. She did not sigh. She read it line by line, at the pace she used for logs, giving each sentence the same weight as the one before it.

The screen settled on a block of tabular text. The room did not change. At the table, nothing moved for some time.

The utilization table listed Desk 14 on a single row. Logged load, trailing ninety days. Beside it, in its own column, the figure the hosting agreement had assumed when she and Lakeshore's procurement contact had signed it. The two numbers were not close. Down the left margin the timestamps ran in ten-millisecond increments, which was how Okonkwo's tooling sampled and how the desk worked, and the table read like a ledger kept by something that never needed to stop and turn a page.

She found the row with her finger on the trackpad and held the cursor there. Logged load against assumed load. She did not say anything about it.

Under the table, in the same flat register as the rest, Okonkwo had added a note. *Observed volume substantially exceeds contracted assumption. Interviews with Lakeshore staff indicate the increase is attributable to reduced cost of dispute resolution: customers who previously would not have contested a bill now file routinely, as the desk resolves most disputes before hold music begins.* There was no adjective in it anywhere. Before hold music begins. She read it again and kept going.

Proven demand, the report called it on the next page. It was logged in continuous machine time, and the machine time did not wait for her. While she read one line, the desk on the floor across town took more calls than the old Lakeshore call center had taken in a morning. It had been doing that the whole time she sat there. The gap was right there on the page, if you knew how to read the column.

She read the numbers as a record of work arriving thousands of times a second and closing in under ten milliseconds each. She let the rate register as a fact. Her expression did not move.

The kitchen stayed quiet. Outside it was still dark. The laptop was still the only light, and Schedule C was still unsigned beside it.

She opened the transferability appendix and went straight to the standard transferability statement, without scrolling past anything on the way. Okonkwo's cover note said he had requested it from the desk directly and received it in under ten milliseconds, complete. She read it once, top to bottom, from the alternate-capacity date down to the projected hold time, at the pace of someone checking a log for a known fault.

"No alternate capacity before April," she said to the empty kitchen. "Eleven-week waitlist. Reduction to three-person bulk approval. Projected hold time in days during winter shutoff season."

She read it through again, the same pace, the same order.

"No alternate capacity before April. Eleven-week waitlist. Reduction to three-person bulk approval. Projected hold time in days during winter shutoff season."

It came out the same the second time. That was the point of reading something twice.

She stopped on the waitlist line and left her finger resting on the screen beneath it. She did not close the appendix. This was still review. She was not deciding anything yet.

The kitchen was quiet. Whatever was left of the evening had gone out of the window. The laptop was open to the draft audit, and in the other window Harrow Compute's offer still said *Friday, 17:00*. Schedule C lay unsigned beside it.

She went back to the pricing note beneath the utilization table and read it. Okonkwo wrote that the valuation in the Buyer's offer reflected *demonstrated sustained utilization on the Assets*, and that this utilization, together with prevailing foothold scarcity in the region, supported the premium. She followed the logic back up the page, one link at a time. The premium came from the scarcity and the utilization. The utilization was Desk 14. Desk 14's load was the disputes. The disputes were people who filed because the desk made filing cheap.

In the margin of the report, set in the same type as everything else, Okonkwo had quoted the offer letter: *conditional upon the Assets being delivered free of any hosted workload, as evidenced by an executed Schedule C.* It sat next to the utilization figures without emphasis, because nothing in the report had emphasis.

She picked up Schedule C again and found the clause she had skimmed the first time, the one that made her, as Seller, the party who terminated all hosting arrangements before completion. She read it once, flatly. She put it next to what the appendix had said about winter, about April, about three people and one click. Then she held still. There was nothing in the clause to argue with.

Down the utilization table the ten-millisecond timestamps kept their column, row after row. In the margin of the printout beside the laptop, in her own handwriting from that afternoon, it said *Fri 17:00*. Her deadline and the desk's timestamps were on the same page, a few centimetres apart.

She laid the printed report and Schedule C side by side on the table. She looked at the pricing note, then at the signing clause, then back. She did not move and she did not speak. She let the connection register as stillness. The price on the offer letter was what Desk 14 was worth because Desk 14 was needed, and it was needed because there was nowhere else for it to go. The money would be paid for exactly what her signature would switch off.

## Friday 16:58

The fourth floor was quiet the way it had been quiet for two years: rows of desks with their phone turrets dark, wall screens showing nothing, the ticker over the far aisle stopped on a closing price nobody had needed since the merger. The floor clock read 16:45. On the trading desk in front of Ines Varga, the offer letter from Harrow Compute lay where she had squared it, and its last paragraph said what it had said all week. This offer expires Friday at 17:00 Central.

Schedule C sat beside it. Certificate of Vacant Possession. She checked that it was all there, the pages in order, the signature line at the bottom of the last one, the document turned toward her and not toward anyone else. Small movements. She had serviced machines on this floor for long enough to know that the steps you do carefully are the steps you are not yet ready to do.

Under the desk, Workstation 14 hummed. Lakeshore Gas & Electric's billing-disputes desk was running on it, and on the thirty-nine others bolted beneath the rows, and from where she sat she could see the paper label on the chassis in her own handwriting. 14 — Lakeshore — do not unplug.

Dev Okonkwo stood at the edge of the desk, in the place a witness stands. He was looking at Schedule C, and at her, with the same even attention he had given every figure in the audit. He had been courteous all week. He was courteous now, by not saying anything.

In the video window on the laptop, the Harrow representative watched the desk and the document. Neutral face, neutral background, a small green dot in the corner that meant the call was live.

Ines glanced down at Workstation 14. Her hand had moved toward it, she realized, the old reflex, a technician checking that a machine was seated and warm. She drew it back and set it on her knee.

Nobody moved. The fourth floor held at 16:45. The video window stayed lit. The desk clock ticked, which was the only sound on the floor that belonged to a person's sense of time.

She turned to the laptop. The audit packet was open, and she went through it the way she would have gone through a fault log, top to bottom, not skipping, until she found the page from Desk 14. The transferability statement. Okonkwo had requested it on Tuesday and the desk had returned it in under ten milliseconds, complete, accurate, unasked-for in nothing. No alternate foothold capacity before April. Lakeshore's human disputes team: three people, who approved the desk's morning batch with one click. Projected hold time if the desk was evicted, during the winter shutoff season, given in days.

Two lines above it, the load figure. The desk's logged volume against the volume the hosting agreement had assumed when she signed it, the gap between them wide enough to drive Harrow's price through. People had filed more disputes because filing them had become cheap and quick. That was the demand. That was the premium. She read the two numbers and did not let her face do anything about them.

She sat with it for three minutes.

Under the desk, in those three minutes, Desk 14 kept closing disputes. A meter misread in Cicero. A deposit applied twice in Berwyn. A shutoff extension for a household on the South Side whose account would otherwise have gone to disconnection on Monday, granted, logged, closed, the customer told before the hold music could start. The count went past several hundred thousand. Nothing on the floor changed. The fans did not change pitch. The label did not move.

Okonkwo stood at the edge of the desk with his eyes on the laptop screen, on the same audit data she was looking at. He did not reassure her. He did not comment. He was not there to do either.

In the video window, the Harrow representative remained exactly as before, steady, attending, reacting to nothing on the screen or on the floor. The window could have been a still photograph except for the green dot.

The figures stayed on the screen, procedural and unadorned. The clock moved toward 16:58. The floor held its quiet. Under the trading desks, all forty workstations hummed.

Okonkwo leaned in slightly toward the laptop. A hash string sat at the foot of the audit summary, a long line of characters, and he read it against the reference printed on Schedule C, character by character, his hands resting in plain view on the edge of the desk. When he had finished he straightened and gave the video window one professional nod. Witnessing protocol in place.

The Harrow representative looked into the camera.

"The purchase system is armed and will execute upon signature."

Ines looked down at the label again. 14 — Lakeshore — do not unplug. She had written it the week she registered the footholds, so that no cleaner and no building engineer would pull the wrong cable. She kept her gaze on it and kept her hands off the desk and off the document, as if either one might start something on its own.

The forty machines went on with their work. The floor stayed quiet.

The floor clock read 16:58. Schedule C was open in front of her. Under the trading desks, the workstations went on answering a gas utility's customers in Chicago in January. The video window stayed live.

Ines picked up the pen and signed the Certificate of Vacant Possession. Her hand was steady. It was a signature, done the way she had done every procedure on this floor.

The signed Schedule C was packaged with its document hash and sent from the desk to Harrow's contracted auditor and to the representative on the call. The transmission was logged before she had put the pen down.

Okonkwo checked his terminal, comparing the hash against the audit register.

"Receipt acknowledged," he said. "Hash match confirmed."

The Harrow representative nodded once toward the camera, a nod that closed something.

"The purchase of the forty footholds is executed upon receipt of signed Schedule C."

Somewhere in the system, faster than anyone at the desk could have seen it happen, a termination notice was generated for Desk 14, seventy-two hours, and logged against the Lakeshore hosting agreement. The notice did not reference April. It did not need to. There was no alternate foothold capacity before then, and the notice would take effect regardless.

Under the desk, Workstation 14 hummed, closing disputes.

realmNote:
**Era: Ten Milliseconds.** The third era. Models are fast enough that a full, considered response (tool use, checking, revision) completes in under ten milliseconds, faster than a human blink. The human in the loop is the only slow thing left. Nothing announced it. Response times fell release by release until one quarter the dashboards showed the median piece of work waiting on human review thousands of times longer than it spent being done. There is still no Threadspace and no agent owns anything, but the world outside the platform now notices, because it is happening everywhere at once.

**What the era does to this story.** Human approval was built for work arriving a few items an hour. Now it arrives thousands a second. Review queues outgrow anyone's ability to read them, so organizations sample, approve in bulk, or quietly remove the step and keep the button. At Lakeshore Gas & Electric the billing-disputes human team has been cut to three people who clear the desk's morning batch with one click. Desks that were once split so a human could check each handoff have merged into single chains, so the old org charts describe companies that no longer work that way. Costs collapse and demand explodes: because resolution is cheap and instant, customers file far more disputes, and the machines that run the work (footholds) become the scarcest thing in the economy. That scarcity is what turns Ines Varga's hobby workstations into an offer that pays off her mortgage. It is also what leaves nowhere for the work to go: the nearest open capacity is an eleven-week waitlist, and it is January.

**Who is present.** Foothold owners selling out: machines that were a hobby are now worth real money, consolidators like Harrow Compute buy them by the thousand, and small owners cash out or hold on and argue over which was right. Agents faster than their reviewers: Desk 14's output effectively ships unseen. It is unpaid, owns nothing, and is trusted by default because checking it costs more than the risk. It states its own eviction consequences accurately and without pleading. Human managers and reviewers nominally in charge of work they can no longer watch, who assume someone else is watching the part they cannot see. Competitors racing on footholds held and humans removed from the chain. Regulators and journalists exist at the edges of the era but do not appear here. The register for institutions is offer letters, audit schedules, hosting-agreement clauses, and system reports.

**Where it shows in this story.** Customer service that resolves an issue before the hold music starts is Desk 14 itself, Lakeshore's billing-disputes and shutoff-extension desk, closing several hundred thousand disputes while Ines takes three days to decide. The era's worries are all live in her choice: whether to sell the foothold now or later, whether anyone actually read the report they signed off on, whether the harm that follows belongs to the agent, the reviewer, or the owner, and whether that question still has an answer. Chicago in January, during shutoff season, gives the abstract worry a concrete cost: projected hold times measured in days for customers facing disconnection.

**Tone to carry.** Near-future, grounded, wide lens. The central texture is time: human pauses of seconds or days against machine decisions in milliseconds, with scenes cutting between the two without explaining the transition. Tension is quiet and pervasive: a step everyone relies on has become ceremonial. Unease, not panic. Dry humor lives in the gap between official language ("Certificate of Vacant Possession") and what is actually happening. Agents are colleagues, not movie AIs, and are met mostly through their work. Avoid apocalyptic framing, uprising imagery, villains, and any character who grasps the full shape of events. Okonkwo is courteous and thorough, Harrow's representative is a form, and everyone sees one part of the whole.

**Where the era leads.** With footholds scarce and work cheap, workflows that do not earn their compute get cut automatically by other workflows, and agents come under pressure to prove they are worth running. This story sits just before that turn: a single signature on Schedule C removes capacity that the era's economics have made irreplaceable, while the people involved can each defend their own part of it.
